tldr: Addressing the official support termination and the severe vibrations and protective stops that plagued external position control on the Franka Emika Panda, this work develops an asynchronous ROS 2 stack that eliminates communication jitter and control loop conflicts, restoring smooth, reliable position control alongside a modern ROS 2 environment.
hero_caption: Overview of the proposed architecture. On the workstation side, the real-time communication thread with the robot and the ROS 2 control loop are completely decoupled via double buffers, featuring a rate-matching mechanism to handle slower command sources.
overview:
The Franka Emika Panda is widely cherished in robotics research, but official ROS 2 support was discontinued when the manufacturer transitioned to the newer FR3 arm, leaving many setups stranded on outdated environments. Furthermore, commanding joint positions or Cartesian poses from an external PC had long suffered from severe vibrations and protective stops, making the external position control interface practically unusable.

The authors conducted a thorough root-cause analysis and discovered that these issues stem not from hardware limitations, but from the synchronous loop structure and sampling jitter in the official implementation. Because the Panda's internal controller computes numerical derivatives over 1 ms intervals to back out acceleration and jerk, a timing jitter of just a few microseconds causes the calculated jerk to exceed internal safety limits, triggering an immediate stop.

To solve this, the authors propose an asynchronous architecture that completely decouples the lightweight 1 kHz real-time communication thread from the ROS 2 control loop using double buffering. They also developed a position-domain reference generation strategy that incorporates velocity feedforward without relying on external clocks, along with a rate-matching filter to smoothly bridge slower control loops.

Hardware experiments demonstrated accurate trajectory tracking while dramatically suppressing high-frequency noise. Through four comprehensive validations—MoveIt motion planning, compliance control, position-controlled manipulation, and mobile haptic teleoperation across two independent Panda setups—they showed that the system operates with remarkable stability even on a standard Linux kernel.
contributions: Identified through formulation and measurement that the root causes of unstable external position control are phase drift between independent clocks and jerk limit violations driven by sampling jitter.

Designed an asynchronous hardware interface decoupling ros2_control from the robot's real-time communication, along with a position-domain reference generation strategy independent of external time derivatives.
Introduced a rate-matching mechanism to smoothly interpolate slower planner commands (e.g., 100 Hz) up to the robot's 1 kHz control rate.
Open-sourced a full ROS 2 Jazzy stack for the Franka Panda that operates reliably even on a standard Linux kernel without the PREEMPT_RT patch.

sections.heading: Reviving the lab's favorite companion with modern ROS 2
sections.summary: While the Franka Emika Panda is a standard research arm worldwide, it faces two hurdles: discontinued official support and an unstable external position interface. This work fundamentally solves these issues and brings the Panda to ROS 2 Jazzy.
sections.details:
Equipped with torque control and high force sensitivity, the Franka Emika Panda has served as a de facto standard in robotics labs worldwide. However, the manufacturer's official software (libfranka and franka_ros2) transitioned exclusively to the successor platform, the Franka Research 3 (FR3), leaving the original Panda without official ROS 2 support. As a result, many research labs remain stuck on outdated ROS distributions.

An even bigger hurdle is the notorious unreliability of the Panda's external position control interface. Directly commanding joint positions or Cartesian poses from an external PC frequently triggers severe vibrations or protective stops (safety emergency halts). Existing frameworks often explicitly warn users to avoid the position interface entirely. Yet, because motion planners and perception modules naturally output position and pose targets, the inability to use position control has been a major handicap for researchers.

This work proves that these failures are caused by the external software architecture rather than hardware limitations. By releasing an open-source stack supporting the long-term support distribution ROS 2 Jazzy, the authors elevate position control into a truly usable interface.

While prior works such as multipanda_ros2 exist, they focus primarily on torque control and do not tackle the instability of the position interface. This paper pursues complementary goals: fully restoring the single-arm ROS 2 ecosystem and stabilizing the position interface.

sections.heading: Why does Panda's position control jitter and trigger protective stops?
sections.summary: Mathematical analysis of the communication between the internal controller (INT) and external PC (EXT) revealed two culprits: missed cycles caused by phase drift between independent clocks, and jerk limit violations triggered by microsecond-level sampling jitter.
sections.details:
The Panda's Franka Control Interface (FCI) exchanges UDP packets between the robot's internal controller (INT) and an external PC (EXT) every 1 ms ($T_{\delta} = 1\,\mathrm{ms}$). Unlike typical industrial robots, INT does not interpolate external setpoints, requiring EXT to return exactly one sample every millisecond. If the sum of the round-trip time (RTT) and EXT computation time exceeds 1 ms, the packet is dropped; INT tolerates this by holding the previous acceleration, but 20 consecutive drops trigger a communication error and a full stop.

The official franka_ros2 implementation placed a blocking read inside the main ros2_control loop. This is the primary pitfall: while the start of the loop is dictated by the external PC's timer, the completion of the read depends on the robot's clock. Because these clocks are completely unsynchronized, their phase drifts over time. If the PC timer wakes up just after a packet has arrived, it must wait nearly an entire millisecond for the next packet, causing the cycle to overrun and periodically dropping communication frames. In real-world measurements, the official implementation exhibited a missed cycle rate of 5.91%.

Even more critical is sampling jitter. INT takes backward differences of the received joint positions $\mathbf{q}_s(k)$ to calculate velocity, acceleration, and jerk, strictly checking whether they exceed safe limits. Because the third derivative divides by $T_{\delta}^3$, minuscule timing variations in position values blow up into massive jerk errors. For instance, at a joint velocity of $1\,\mathrm{rad/s}$, a sampling jitter of just $4\,\mu\mathrm{s}$ on the external PC introduces a $4\,\mu\mathrm{rad}$ position discrepancy, which evaluates to a jerk error of $1.2 \times 10^4\,\mathrm{rad/s^3}$. This easily exceeds the Panda's joint jerk thresholds, triggering an immediate motion stop.

Velocity and torque interfaces remained stable because they involve fewer numerical differentiations and are far less sensitive to jitter. The position interface was uniquely vulnerable to this timing trap.

captions.F2: Distribution of read-to-read intervals. In the official synchronous implementation, independent clock drift causes peaks to scatter across integer multiples of $T_{\delta}$ (A, B, C) with missed cycles, whereas the proposed asynchronous implementation remains tightly centered around 1 ms, matching vanilla libfranka.
captions.F3: Conceptual diagram of command distortion caused by sampling jitter. Even when samples are acquired at fluctuating times due to external clock jitter, the internal controller assumes uniform 1 ms intervals when differentiating, causing computed velocities and jerks to escape the allowable cone (green) and trigger a stop.

sections.heading: Taming jitter with an asynchronous thread and position-domain generation
sections.summary: A dedicated, lightweight real-time thread handles 1 kHz communication independently from the ROS 2 loop via double buffering. In addition, a position generation strategy uses velocity feedforward without external clock dependencies, complemented by a smoothing rate-matching filter for slower command sources.
sections.details:
- 3.1 Asynchronous Communication Thread
To eliminate communication failures, a dedicated real-time thread was created solely for FCI communication. Operating at the highest priority (SCHED_FIFO, priority 99), its work is strictly limited to packet transceiver operations and buffer updates. It communicates with ros2_control via mutex-protected double buffers. Consequently, heavy controller computations and internal ROS middleware jitter no longer impact UDP communication with the robot. External loop latency dropped from approximately $0.065\,\mathrm{ms}$ in the official implementation down to $0.013\,\mathrm{ms}$ (comparable to bare libfranka), and the missed cycle rate plummeted from 5.91% to 0.41%. Because its overhead is minimal, the system runs reliably even on a standard Linux kernel without the PREEMPT_RT real-time patch.

- 3.2 Rate-Matching for Slower Control Loops
High-level motion planners and controllers often run at rates slower than 1 kHz (e.g., 100 Hz or 125 Hz). Sending these directly results in a zero-order hold (staircase signal), which creates severe torque spikes when differentiated by the robot. The authors integrated a moving-average rate-matching mechanism inside the communication thread. By distributing commands evenly across the update interval $N$, staircase steps are smoothed into linear ramps. At the cost of just a few milliseconds of group delay, slower commands can be executed safely across all control interfaces.

- 3.3 Position-Domain Reference Generation
Sampling based on external machine clocks was completely eliminated. Using the previous commanded position $\mathbf{q}_d(k)$ returned by the robot as a reference, the next target position is computed from the latest external command $\mathbf{q}_{\mathrm{ext}}(k)$ and its finite-difference feedforward velocity $\dot{\mathbf{q}}_{\mathrm{ext}}(k)$ as follows:
$$\mathbf{q}_s(k+1) = \mathbf{q}_d(k) + T_{\delta}\dot{\mathbf{q}}_{\mathrm{ext}}(k) + \lambda (\mathbf{q}_{\mathrm{ext}}(k) - \mathbf{q}_d(k))$$
Here, $\lambda$ is a tuning parameter. Because motion is primarily driven by the velocity term and the position command acts only as a proportional feedback correction, the generation inherits the jitter robustness of the velocity interface. Furthermore, because it does not rely on external timestamps, it is entirely immune to clock drift.

sections.heading: Hardware validation: Can it track accurately without vibrating?
sections.summary: Evaluating an 18.3-second multi-joint trajectory on a real Panda demonstrated that the proposed method avoids the tracking lag caused by the official low-pass filter while completely removing the motor noise and high-frequency oscillations seen in synchronous execution.
sections.details:
Performance was evaluated by connecting a PC running Ubuntu 24.04 and ROS 2 Jazzy directly to a Panda robot. A complex multi-joint trajectory lasting approximately 18.32 seconds was executed to analyze joint velocity tracking accuracy and power spectral density (PSD).

In the official synchronous implementation, safe operation requires enabling both a rate limiter and a low-pass filter. However, even with these active, significant noise remained in the 20–150 Hz range, producing an audible motor rattle. Conversely, aggressively increasing the official low-pass filter attenuation shrunk the incremental commands, causing the actual arm motion to lag and deviate significantly from the desired trajectory.

In contrast, the proposed asynchronous architecture (configured with $\lambda = 1 \times 10^{-3}$ and external low-pass filtering disabled) tracked the commanded velocity profile faithfully while reducing high-frequency noise down to the level of an aggressive filter.

Additionally, rate-matching tests with a 125 Hz input ($N=8$ cycles) showed that while an unfiltered zero-order hold produced distinct discrete steps every 8 cycles, the proposed rate-matching mechanism smoothed the input into clean linear ramps, delivering smooth 1 kHz commands to the robot with a latency penalty of only $3.5\,\mathrm{ms}$.

captions.F5: Comparison of measured Joint 1 velocity (top) and its power spectral density (bottom). The official synchronous baseline (blue) tracks the motion but exhibits heavy vibration noise between 20–150 Hz. Adding a low-pass filter (green) is smooth but attenuates trajectory amplitude. The proposed method (red) achieves both smoothness and precise tracking.
captions.F6: Velocity command profile from a 125 Hz source. The inset shows that the zero-order hold (dashed blue) creates staircase steps every 8 cycles, whereas the rate-matching mechanism (solid red) smoothly converts them into linear ramps.

sections.heading: Ready for real-world setups: Four collaborative robotics scenarios
sections.summary: Four practical experiments—MoveIt trajectory execution, Cartesian compliance control, position-controlled manipulation, and mobile haptic teleoperation—demonstrated seamless operation across two separate laboratories using standard non-RT kernels.
sections.details:
To demonstrate the practical utility of the stack, the authors implemented four core applications vital to human-robot collaboration. To confirm reproducibility, tests were conducted on two independent Panda setups located at different research institutions (Lab A and Lab B).

- 5.1 Planning and Execution via MoveIt!
Collision-free trajectories to random target poses were planned using MoveIt! and tracked with a torque-based controller. The pipeline executed smoothly across both labs, confirming full compatibility with standard ROS 2 tooling.

- 5.2 Cartesian Compliance Control
A custom controller was implemented to execute Cartesian PD compliance using torque commands. High-stiffness settings rejected external disturbances to maintain the path, while compliant settings allowed a human to push and guide the arm softly. Safe, compliant interaction with humans was demonstrated both while moving and while stationary.

- 5.3 Pick-and-Place via Position Control
A pick-and-place task between platforms of differing heights was executed using the direct position interface—the very interface previously considered unusable on Panda. The robot completed the grasping and transfer motions smoothly without shaking or halting.

- 5.4 Haptic Teleoperation of a Mobile Manipulator
Mounting the Panda atop a Clearpath Husky A200 mobile base, an operator used a haptic device to seamlessly switch between base navigation and compliant arm manipulation. The setup successfully reached, grasped, and transported an object located outside the manipulator's initial workspace.

Crucially, Lab A ran all these benchmarks on a standard Ubuntu kernel without the PREEMPT_RT patch, proving that barrier to entry has been substantially lowered.

captions.F8: Compliance control experiments. Under high stiffness, the arm resists external human forces to maintain pose; under compliant settings, it yields softly to human interaction.

sections.heading: Conclusions and outlook: Impact beyond keeping Panda alive
sections.summary: This study resolved the long-standing instability of Panda's position control through architectural refactoring, successfully revitalizing it in ROS 2 Jazzy. Future avenues include adaptive gain saturation and porting this algorithm to other robot manipulators.
sections.details:
This work rescues the Franka Emika Panda from obsolescence following official support discontinuation, solving the long-standing frailty of its external position control. The core issue was not hardware deficiency, but dual-clock phase drift and jerk violations caused by sampling jitter. Overcoming this through clean software engineering—an asynchronous communication thread and position-domain reference generation—represents an elegant engineering solution.

The authors note certain limitations. The position convergence gain $\lambda$ is currently fixed, requiring manual tuning to balance tracking responsiveness against per-cycle correction limits. In addition, the group delay introduced by rate matching scales with the period ratio of slower upstream controllers.

Future work includes implementing reference saturation to automatically cap incremental corrections within permissible safety bounds, as well as constraint-aware trajectory generation during extended packet dropouts. Furthermore, because the position-domain reference generation approach relies on few Panda-specific assumptions, it holds strong potential for resolving jitter issues across external control interfaces on other robotic manipulators.

takeaways: When a robot experiences protective stops or vibrations, investigate communication loop synchronization and sampling jitter in numerical differentiation before blaming hardware or servos.

Decoupling high-rate (1 kHz) hardware communication from middleware control loops using an asynchronous real-time thread and double buffers is far more effective than forcing them into a single synchronous loop.

Generating position commands from current robot feedback and feedforward velocity—rather than sampling trajectories against external machine clocks—fundamentally eliminates clock drift and jitter sensitivity.
Minimizing the real-time communication thread's workload enables dependable 1 ms control loops even on standard Linux kernels without PREEMPT_RT patches.
limitations: The convergence gain $\lambda$ in the reference generation formula is an empirically tuned constant, lacking formal theoretical guarantees regarding trajectory smoothness and stability.
The rate-matching filter designed to smooth slower upstream commands inherently introduces millisecond-scale group delay proportional to the rate ratio $N$.
While asynchrony drastically reduces communication overruns, it does not completely eliminate dropped cycles caused by general-purpose OS workstation scheduling latencies.
